How to play:
Your target number is 50. This is the total that both players are trying to make.
Player 1 rolls the dice above. They can choose whether to double the number shown or halve the number shown.

Botticelli
How to play:
Player 1 thinks of a famous person.
The person can be real or fictional, alive or dead. They should be someone both players have heard of.
Player 1 then tells Player 2 the first letter of their person’s name.
Usually this will be the first letter of their surname, e.g. “R” for Christiano Ronaldo or “O” for Michelle Obama, though sometimes a person is known by their first name alone, so you would need to use that letter instead, e.g. “L” for Lorde or “A” for Adele.
Player 2 must think of a person it could be and ask a question that could give that person as the answer.
E.g. if the letter was “D”, then the person could be Roald Dahl, so they could ask, “Are you a children’s author?”
Player 1 must then answer the question.
There are four possible things that could happen:
Player 1 answers, “No, I am not Roald Dahl.” Player 2 will then need to ask more questions.
Player 1 answers, “No, I am not Julia Donaldson.” This might mean their person is Roald Dahl but further questions would be needed to check.
Player 1 can’t think of an alternative as in example ii, and so is forced to answer, “Yes, I am Roald Dahl” and Player 2 wins.
Player 1 can’t think of a children’s author beginning “D” and so has to say, “No, and I don’t know who you are thinking of.” If this happens, Player 2 must say who they were thinking of, and then they are allowed to ask one yes/no question about the person to help narrow down who it could be.
Player 2 keeps asking questions until they have found out who it is.
If it starts becoming too difficult, Player 1 can say who their person was and they win the

The Game:
Imagine you are both at a party. The Host is welcoming guests and talking to them. But one guest arrives and the Host does not know who they are. This new person is the Mystery Visitor! Choose one person to be the Host and one person to be the Mystery Visitor.

Simon says
In the game ‘Simon Says’, there are two kinds of instructions:
Instructions that begin ‘Simon says’.
Instructions that do not begin ‘Simon says’.
The person following the instructions must listen carefully:
If the instruction begins ‘Simon says,’ they should follow it.
If the instruction does not begin ‘Simon says,’ they should not follow it.

Inventing a Poem
Have a go at inventing your own poem and then performing it, either to someone at home, over the phone or by filming yourself.Here are two ideas to get you started (but you can write any kind of poem you like):
Idea 1

Idea 2
Talk with your pen. This sounds like a funny idea, but it’s the kind of thing Michael Rosen does in lots of his poems, including ‘Strict’ in Activity 1. Talking with your pen is where you just write down some thoughts or ideas, maybe about something you’ve seen or heard.

Michael Rosen turns these ideas into poems partly through the way he repeats lines. See if you can include some repetition to turn your thoughts into a poem.

Should Everything be Free?
Read this question ↑ and then talk about it together.This conversation is called a discussion. In a discussion, you should:
Make sure both people have a chance to talk.
Listen to what the other person has to say.
Be polite to each other, including valuing what the other person says (though this doesn’t mean you always have to agree).
Respond to what the other person says, maybe saying, “I agree because…” or “I disagree because…”
Build on what the other person says.
Keep on topic – don’t start talking about something else!
Explain your opinions with reasons.
Speak loudly enough for the other person to hear you but not so loudly they don’t want to listen.

World Cup of Children’s Books
Setting up:
Choose sixteen children’s books that could potentially win the competition ‘Best Children’s Book of All Time’. Remember, it can include any children’s books you like, including picture books and novels. It is fun to have a mix! Make sure you both know all the books!

Keep going until all the ‘Last Sixteen’ spaces are filled.How to play:
For each pair of books, each player must choose a book to support.
Think of reasons why your book is better than the other.
Debate which book should go through to the next round, sharing your reasons. You need to argue for your book, but eventually you will need to come to an agreement.
Write the winning book in the ‘Quarter Finals’ space.
Repeat with the other books in the ‘Last Sixteen’ round so you end up with eight quarter-finalists.
Once you have all your quarter-finalists, repeat the process with your new pairs to see which four books go through to the Semi Finals.
Repeat your debate with your semi-finalists to fund your two finalists.
Debate your two finalists to find out who wins the award ‘Best Children’s Book of All Time’!

Something to write with

An adult and child koala sitting together on a sofa with a book.Activity:

Ideas of some questions to discuss:

Explaining to an Alien
In this activity, you will be giving someone a really clear explanation to help them do something. You need to choose an everyday task for the activity that you don’t mind doing twice!What to do:
Choose an everyday task, e.g. brushing your teeth.
Explain to the other person how to do it.
While you are explaining, they should do the task. They should your instructions carefully.
Watch closely what they are doing – are your instructions easy to follow?
Now imagine the other person is an alien who has never brushed their teeth before, or even seen a toothbrush or sink.
Explain how to do the task again, but this time make sure the instructions are something that an alien would be able to follow.
While you are explaining, they should pretend to be an alien and do the task. They might get things wrong if your explanation is not clear!
Tip for Grownups:
When you are pretending to be the alien, you can pretend to misunderstand any instructions which are unclear. Your child might have to explain in a different way to help you understand!

Find a Balance
What to Do:
Choose a topic you do not agree on (or you can pretend you don’t agree). See below for some ideas.
Stand opposite each other at different sides of the room (you should be fairly far apart).
Player 1 says her side of the argument.
Player 2 says his side of the argument.
Player 1 thinks of something she could do to help settle the differences between them.
Player 2 thinks about this offer and says why (or why not) he is prepared to accept this proposal.
If Player 2 accepts the proposal, Player 1 takes a step forward. If Player 2 does not accept the proposal, Player 1 stays still.
Now Player 2 thinks of something she could do to help settle the differences between them and Player 1 says why (or why not) she is prepared to accept it. If Player 1 accepts the offer, Player 2 takes a step forward.
Keep repeating this, taking turns to suggest something, until you are close enough to shake hands. When this happens, you have found a workable compromise and can shake hands on your settlement.
Debate topicsThe Aim of the Game:
To start with a topic on which you do not agree, then to share your side of the argument, listen to the other person’s ideas, and then come to a {{definition "compromise" "This is when you meet somewhere in the middle. It might not be the perfect answer for either person, but it should be an ok resolution for both of you."}}.

Activity Name: I notice / I think / I wonder
Page Contents:
I notice / I think / I wonder
The activity:
Tell your child that you've found this interesting thing or picture and you want to chat about it.
Begin by saying "I notice…" and completing the sentence with something you notice, e.g. if it is a sieve, "I notice it has lots of little holes in it."
Ask what they notice and encourage them to start their answer with "I notice".
You could do a couple of things you notice each.
Repeat with "I think" and "I wonder".
Note:
I notice is things you can see (or feel or smell or hear).
I think is ideas you have about it and things you can work out.
I wonder is things you want to know or are not sure about.
For this activity you will need an object or a picture.

The Best Book Ever
The Activity:
Both people should do the activity.
Decide which book you think is the best book ever. You can talk together or think on your own.
Think of some reasons that it is the best book ever. If you want, you could make some notes to help you remember your ideas. Here are some things you could think about:
What did you enjoy about it?
Do other people like it?
Is there anything you can learn from it?
What is important about this book?
Are there any other books like it?
Why is it better than the other books you talked about in the warmup?
Explain to the other person why your book is the best book ever.
Listen to what the other person has to say.
Talk together about why you agreed or disagreed on the best book. Is it possible for there to be only one best book?
Warmup:
Can you think of any really good books? Make a short list together and talk about what you think makes them really good.

All About Me
One-minute first ideas:
Think about the type of presentation you want to do – are you going to do “A History of Me” from when you were born to now, or are you going to do something about how you are now?
Think about the important things to include – some of it might be facts, like your age or what foods you like, and some of it might be trickier to explain, like your feelings about particular things or what your personality is like. You can decide what you want to share, and what you think is important.
Two-minute planning:
Make notes of what you are going to say. Don’t write every single word, because presentations sound better when you speak rather than read out your notes.
Two-minute practising:
Practise saying your words a few times. This will help you check if it feels about the right length, and also make sure your notes help you remember everything you want to say.
One-minute presentation:
Decide who is going to go first. The other person will get to speak afterwards!
Make sure you speak clearly so your audience can hear what you are saying.
Use your notes to help you remember what to say!
When you’ve finished, spend a minute listening to the other person’s presentation.
The Activity:

Cover of a Book
In this activity, you are both rival designers for a book publisher. You will both be designing a cover for a new book, competing to see whose title and blurb will be chosen for the final book!Before you Start:
Work together to decide which book you are designing the cover for. Here are some ideas:
A book you have both read
A TV series you have both watched
A film you have both seen
Something else!
Choose something you both know pretty well so you can imagine what the book might say inside. But don’t choose something with a cover you remember, otherwise you might accidentally copy the original!
What to Do:
The winner will be the person who comes up with the best title and blurb for the book. You can design the pictures and layout if you want, but don’t forget that the competition is all about the words!
On a piece of paper, write a new title for the book.
Don’t use the original title.
Think carefully what the book is about and make sure the title fits.
Keep it quite short so it is easy to see.
Try and make it interesting or exciting so that it makes someone want to read the book.
Below the title, write a new blurb for the book.
A blurb is usually between 100 and 200 words long. Try to stick to this!
Remember that a blurb is trying to tempt someone to read the book – it should make the person want to read more.
The blurb needs to show what is in the book without giving too much away – it would be rubbish if the blurb told you the ending!
Make sure the blurb matches the tone of the book – if the book is exciting, it needs to be exciting, but if the book is a serious non-fiction text, you might need something more serious.
When you have finished, read through and check you work. You might decide to make some changes and improvements.
When you have both finished, read each other’s title and blurb. Talk together about what you like and compare what you have both written. Which will win? Why?

Haiku Stories
A haiku is a short poem originally from Japan. It has a very strict structure with three lines. The first line has five syllables, the second line has seven syllables and the third line has five syllables.Here is an example:The Activity:
Write your own Haiku story. Both of you should write one, and then guess which story the other person’s Haiku is about!
Choose a story. It’s easier if it’s a story that lots of people know. Fairy tales work well!
Think about the important parts of the story – what must you include to help them guess? Try not to include the story title though – that would be too easy!
Try saying your ideas and count the syllables on your fingers as you say them. When you have something that works, write it down. It might not end up in your final poem, but you don’t want to forget it.
Try out lots of ideas until you are happy with your poem as a whole. Then write down the finished haiku.
When you have both finished, read your haikus aloud and try to guess which stories they come from!
Example:
Can you guess which story this haiku is telling?
In a pumpkin coach,
To the ball. Clock strikes twelve but…
The glass slipper fits!
Silver moonlight shines.
Only a dormouse rustles
In the silent night.

Fold-over stories
How to Play:
Player 1 writes the first line of a story. The last bit of the line goes on the line/space below as a “hook” for the next person to finish. Make sure it is an unfinished sentence so that the first thing they need to do is finish the sentence.
Player 2 finishes the sentence and starts a new one, again leaving a “hook” on the next line.
Keep swapping over until you get to the end.
Unfold the paper and see what story you have written!
How to Make it Really Good:
Don’t get stuck with the story you started telling. If you keep trying to go back to your first idea, it won’t really work. Instead, use the other person’s “hook” to move on your ideas, which will keep changing each time you add something.
Don’t peek at what the other person wrote. It doesn’t matter if it makes sense. In fact, it can be funnier if it doesn’t!

In this game, you will be trying to sneak one lie past the other player.How to Play

Cereal Box Speech Bubbles
Writing 1:
Swap bubbles with the other person and write what they said on a piece of paper.
If it ends with a ? or ! you can leave it as it is, but if it ends with a full stop you will need to change it to a comma.
Add in your speech marks.
Write who said it after the speech (and how) – this is called the ‘reporting clause’. Remember, you don't need a capital letter to start the reporting clause when it comes after the speech.
Remember to end your sentence with some punctuation too!
Writing 2:
Using the same speech bubbles, see if you can put the reporting clause at the start of the sentence, e.g. Mum shouted, "....."

Talk about these questions together:
Is it the first paragraph or does it follow something else?
Is there another paragraph after it?
How long is it?
How does it start?
What tense is it written in?
How does the second sentence link to the first sentence? Is it with a pronoun or an adverbial or something else?
Does the third sentence link back to the second sentence? How?
Does the third sentence link back to the first sentence? How?
Why did the writer end the paragraph there?You Will Need:

A book

Fold-Over Paragraphs
Editing:
Choose one paragraph each. Edit your paragraph so that it all works together. Here are some things to look for:
Look for really long sentences which need to be split into several parts.
Look for extra words that are not needed when you read the whole sentence.
Check that the whole paragraph is written in the same tense (unless there is a good reason it shouldn’t be).
Check that the pronouns (he, she, it etc) make sense.
Check that singular and plural nouns match the verb they are doing, e.g. one horse runs but two horses run.
Think about adding or changing some adverbials to link the sentences together.
Decide whether you need to add anything so that it makes sense.
You Will Need:
Two things to write with.
Two pieces of lined paper (draw your own lines onto plain paper if you need to).
Writing:
Begin writing your paragraph. It can be about anything you like.
When you get to the end of the first line on the page, skip a line and write two more words on the next line.
Fold over the paper so you can’t see the first line of writing but you can still see the two words on the next line.
Swap paper.
Keep writing from the two words you can see. When you get to the end of the line on the page, skip a line again and again write two more words on the next line.
Keep swapping over, writing and folding until you have done ten lines.
Swap one last time, but this time finish the sentence. You can keep going over the end of a line if you need to.
Swap over one last time and unfold the paper. Read your two paragraphs aloud to each other. Did they make you laugh?
This game is about taking it in turns to write lines to make a paragraph. But you won’t see what the person has written before you! It might get silly!

How to Play:
Player 1 starts reading from the book. They could begin at the start or somewhere in the middle. It is probably best to begin at the start of a chapter or section though!

Target Words
Other Rules for Giving CluesYou Will Need:
A 4x6 playing grid with words on.
A card showing you 9 target words and 3 poison words to avoid.
Two colours of counters to cover words you have guessed.
Call one set of counters ‘target counters’ and one set of counters ‘other counters’.
You could use two types of coin, buttons, pasta or anything you like.
The Aim of the Game:
Player 1 gives single-word clues for the target words and Player 2 tries to guess them in as few turns as possible without accidentally choosing any of the other words. If Player 2 guesses a poison word, the game ends!
How to Play
Put a word grid on the table or floor between you.
Player 1 looks at a target word card to see which words are target words, which words they should avoid, and which are the three poison words. They must not show the card to Player 2.
Player 1 gives a single-word clue that relates to some of the target words. Player 1 also gives a number to say how many words relate to the clue. E.g. two of your words are ‘sand’ and ‘sea’ and both of these are part of a beach, so you say, ‘Beach: 2.’
Player 2 thinks about the clue and talks about their thinking out loud. Player 1 is not allowed to say anything or give any face or movement hints to help. Listening to Player 2 is useful though, as it can help you understand their thinking ready for giving the next clue.
When Player 2 has decided on a word (or words), they touch one word on the grid.
If it was a target word, put a 'target counter' on the word. Player 2 may guess another word (up to the number given by Player 1 in the clue).
If it was a poison word, the game ends.
If it was another word, put an ‘other counter’ on the word. The turn ends.
On  the next turn, Player 1 gives a new clue.
Keep track of how many clues are given before all the target words are found.
At the end of the game, add together your number of clues given and the number of ‘other words’ accidentally guessed. This is your score for the game. The lower the score, the better! If you accidentally guessed a poison word, the game ended with a high score of infinity!
Play again but swapping roles so the other person has a chance to give the clues. See if you can beat your score!
Important Rule:
The player giving the clues is not allowed to help in any other way – they can’t comment on their own clues (e.g. ‘this is maybe a bit of a stretch), they can’t comment on the other player’s choices, they can’t even move their face!!

Accept: To agree to receive, e.g. “He accepted the pen as a present.”
Affect: to have an effect on or make a difference to, e.g. “The damp began to affect my health.”
Ball: A sphere that you play with, e.g. “I threw him the ball.”
Bawl: Cry loudly, e.g. “The baby began to bawl.”
Berry: A kind of small fruit, e.g. “There was a juicy, red berry on the raspberry bush.”
Brake: What you do to slow down a car or bike (or the thing you use to do that), e.g. “Squeeze the brake to slow done your bike!”
Break: Damage, e.g. “If you drop the box of eggs, they will break.”
Bury: Cover with soil underground, e.g. “The pirate dug a hole to bury the treasure.”
Effect: A change which is the result of an action or other cause, e.g. “The warm weather had a positive effect on my health.”
Except: Not including, other than, e.g. “I work every day except Saturday.”
Fair: Treating people in an equal way, e.g. “I’ll be fair – you can have five sweets each.”
Fare: What you pay when you get on a bus or train, e.g. “The driver asked for the fare and I paid £3.50.”
Grate: What you do to cheese (or other food) using a grater to make little bits, e.g. “Please can you grate some cheese onto my pasta?”
Great: Another word for amazing, e.g. “You have drawn a great picture of mum!”
Groan: Make a deep inarticulate sound conveying pain or despair, e.g. “Ben groaned and pulled the duvet over his head.”
Grown: Got bigger, e.g. “The sunflower had grown another 6cm!”
He’ll: Short for “he will”, e.g. “I think he’ll come to the shops with me.”
Heal: When a hurt gets better, e.g. “I cut my hand but it will heal soon.
Hear: What you do with your ears to sense sound, e.g. “I can hear the phone ringing.”
Heel: The back part of a foot or shoe, e.g. “There is a hole in the heel of my sock.”
Here: The place where you are, e.g. “Here is my shoe!”
Knot: What you get if you tie string together, e.g. “Tie a knot in the rope to stop the boat floating away.”
Mail: Another word for post or letters, e.g. “I got a parcel in the mail!”
Main: The most important one, e.g. “The main road runs through the middle of town.”
Male: The opposite of female, e.g. “A male lion has a mane.”
Mane: The hair on the head of a horse or male lion, e.g. “The horse flicked its mane out of its eyes.”
Meat: Food made from the flesh of an animal, e.g. “Tigers eat meat but sheep do not.”
Medal: Usually a metal disc on a ribbon given as a prize, e.g. “She got a gold medal for winning the race.
Meddle: Interfere in something that is nothing to do with you, e.g. “Do not meddle in other people’s affairs.”
Meet: Come together, e.g. “Let’s meet outside the coffee shop.”
Missed: Didn’t hit or didn’t catch, e.g. “I missed the train.”
Mist: Light fog or low cloud, e.g. “The mist in the valley was cold and grey.”
Not: This makes something the opposite or negative, e.g. “That is not my cat.”
Peace: Quiet, calm, the opposite of war, e.g. “I enjoyed five minutes peace before the children came home.”
Piece: A bit of something, e.g. “I ate a large piece of chocolate cake.”
Plain: Not decorated, basic, e.g. “I like eating plain food.”
Plane: Short for “aeroplane”, e.g. “I flew in an aeroplane to France.”
Rain: Water that falls from the sky, e.g. “I put up my umbrella to keep off the rain.”
Reign: The period of time when a king or queen is in charge, e.g. “Queen Victoria’s reign lasted 63 years and seven months.”
Rein: The strap a rider uses to control a horse, e.g. “I pulled on the rein to stop my horse.”
Scene: The place where something real or fictional happened, e.g. “First, the author set the scene by describing what the cottage was like.”
Seen: Observed something with your eyes, e.g. “Have you seen my socks?”
Weather: The conditions outside, e.g. “The weather today was cold and snowy.”
Whether: Expresses a choice or an alternative, e.g. “I had to decide whether to put on my coat.”
Who’s: short for “who is”, e.g. “Who’s going to set the table?”
Whose: a possessive pronoun, like “my” which asks or tells who something belongs to, e.g. “Whose shoes are these?”

Up the dictionary
Two acornsIn this game, you will use your knowledge of the alphabet to think of words and try to beat the other player! 
How to play:
Player 1 thinks of a five-letter word beginning with A, e.g. “acorn”.
Player 2 thinks of another five-letter word that follows these two rules:
It comes later in the dictionary than the previous word;
It contains at least one “crash” with the previous word (it has one letter the same in the same position in the word). For example, “broth” could follow “acorn” because it has an “o” as its third letter.
Player 2 then thinks of another word following these two rules, e.g. “couch” could follow “broth” because it has an “h” as its fifth letter.
Keep taking it in turns to think of another word. The winner is the last player who is able to say a word.

Double or don't?
admit → admitting / admitted → the last syllable is stressed so double the last consonant then add the suffix
happen → happening / happened → the last syllable is unstressed so just add the suffix
visit → visiting / visited / visitation → the last syllable is unstressed so just add the suffix
enter → entering / entered → the last syllable is unstressed so just add the suffix
hike → hiking / hiked / hiker → the word ends with e so take off the e then add the suffix
prepare → preparing / prepared / preparation → the word ends with e so take off the e then add the suffix
sense → sensing / sensed / sensation → the word ends with e so take off the e then add the suffix
affix → affixing / affixed → even though the last syllable is stressed, the word ends with x so just add the suffix
carry → carrying / carried / carrier → the word ends with y so if the suffix starts with e you need to take off the e before adding the suffix
uncross → uncrossing / uncrossed → the word ends with two consonants so just add the suffix
upset → upsetting → the last syllable is stressed so double the last consonant then add the suffix
shake → shaking / shaker / shaken → the word ends with e so take off the e then add the suffixChallenge:
Are there any other rules you need to think about when adding the suffixes to these words?

Describing words
A child koala explaining something to an adult koala.The suffix 'ation' is added at the end of {{definition "verbs" "Verbs are doing words, e.g. 'run' or 'clap'."}} to form {{definition "nouns" "Nouns are the names of things, e.g. 'car' or 'octopus'."}} . This game is all about thinking about what the nouns mean.
Cancellation - something that has been cancelled and will no longer happen, e.g. a bus journey.
Commendation - a piece of formal or official praise.
Desertification - the process of an area of land turning into a desert.
Duration - the length of time something lasts.
Electrification - the process of making something electric, e.g. a railway.
Exhalation - the process of breathing out.
Experimentation - the process of doing an experiment.
Exploitation - the act of treating someone unfairly in order to benefit from their work.
Generalisation - a general statement that can be applied to lots of things based on a specific case.
Hospitalisation - the process of becoming ill or injured in a way that means you have to go into hospital.
Information - facts about something.
Improvisation - the act of making something up on the spot.
Inspiration - the process of being mentally stimulated to do something, especially something creative.
Nationalisation - the process of becoming run by the nation or government.
Objectification - the action of making a person seem less valuable by treating them like an object.
Organisation - an organised group of people who are together for a purpose, e.g. a business.
Perspiration - another word for sweat.
Prioritisation - the process of deciding which things are more important to do first.
Respiration - the process of gases being used by an animal or plant to create energy.
Starvation - the suffering caused by a serious lack of food.
Temptation - the desire to do something, particularly something wrong or unwise.
Transplantation - the process of moving a plant to a new piece of soil or an organ to a new body, e.g. a kidney transplant.
Transportation - the process of moving something from one place to another.
Valuation - an estimation of how much money something is worth.

A bag with characters inside, including Spongebob Squarepants, Big Bird, and Peter Pan.Name suggestionsToo tricky?
Take it in turns to describe a person from the bag without using the timer. This is a bit more of a relaxing way to play, with no winner or loser at the end. 
How to play:
Start the timer.
Player 1 takes a name out of the bag.
Player 1 describes the person to player 2. 
Player 2 must try to guess the person.
When Player 2 guesses correctly, Player 1 starts describing the next person.
Keep describing until the time runs out.
Any names that have not been guessed when the time runs out should be put back in the bag. 
Player 1 (the person describing) should keep all the names that were correctly guessed.
Swap over so that Player 2 can describe.
Keep swapping until all the names have been guessed.
The winner is the player with the most names collected at the end of the game.
